\section[lo scippo]{lo scippo — the bag-snatching}

\label{lesson:IT-C291-scippo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the victim, then the Italian for to commit.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: lo scippo}
\textbf{lo scippo} — \textquotedblleft{}the bag-snatching\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Alla stazione c'è stato uno scippo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There was a bag-snatching at the station.}
\end{quote}

A theft from the hand, often by someone on a moped; common on the local news.

\begin{cousinweb}
The origin of \emph{scippo} is not settled; it is usually linked with southern Italian dialect words for snatching (EtymDB has no entry).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for the victim, then the Italian for to commit, then say \emph{lo scippo} again

\section[scippare]{scippare — to snatch (a bag) from someone}

\label{lesson:IT-C291-scippare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to commit, then the Italian for the bag-snatching.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: scippare}
\textbf{scippare} — \textquotedblleft{}to snatch (a bag) from someone\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Un ragazzo in moto le ha scippato la borsa.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{A boy on a motorbike snatched her bag.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Scippare qualcosa a qualcuno}.

\begin{cousinweb}
The origin of \emph{scippare} is not settled; it is the verb behind \emph{scippo} and is usually traced to southern dialects (EtymDB has no entry).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[il borseggiatore]{il borseggiatore — the pickpocket}

\label{lesson:IT-C291-borseggiatore}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the bag-snatching, then the Italian for to snatch.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il borseggiatore}
\textbf{il borseggiatore} — \textquotedblleft{}the pickpocket\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Attenzione ai borseggiatori sull'autobus!
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Watch out for pickpockets on the bus!}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{borsa}, ‘bag’: someone who goes through your bag.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{borseggiatore} is built on \emph{borseggiare} \textquotedblleft{}to pick pockets\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{borsa} \textquotedblleft{}bag\textquotedblright{}, which is usually traced to Late Latin \emph{bursa} \textquotedblleft{}a purse\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[derubare]{derubare — to rob someone, to steal from}

\label{lesson:IT-C291-derubare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to snatch, then the Italian for the pickpocket.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: derubare}
\textbf{derubare} — \textquotedblleft{}to rob someone, to steal from\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
In vacanza ci hanno derubato.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We were robbed on holiday.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Derubare} takes the person, \emph{rubare} the thing: \emph{mi hanno derubato}, \emph{mi hanno rubato il portafoglio}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{derubare} is built on \emph{rubare} \textquotedblleft{}to steal\textquotedblright{}; EtymDB links it with French \emph{dérober} \textquotedblleft{}to steal\textquotedblright{}, from Old French \emph{desrober}. \emph{Rubare} goes back, through Medieval Latin, to a Frankish word for plunder (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la refurtiva]{la refurtiva — the stolen goods}

\label{lesson:IT-C291-refurtiva}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the pickpocket, then the Italian for to rob someone.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la refurtiva}
\textbf{la refurtiva} — \textquotedblleft{}the stolen goods\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La polizia ha trovato la refurtiva in un garage.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The police found the stolen goods in a garage.}
\end{quote}

A police and news word, singular only.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{refurtiva} is usually traced to Latin \emph{rēs fūrtīva} \textquotedblleft{}a stolen thing\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{fūrtīvus} \textquotedblleft{}stolen\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{fūrtum} \textquotedblleft{}theft\textquotedblright{} and \emph{fūr} \textquotedblleft{}thief\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
